subject: Cognitive Science
title: Phonemes: The Atoms of Speech
description: A short lesson to help you apply Phonemes: The Atoms of Speech.

hook.text: English has about 44 distinct sounds. Japanese has about 25. Each language carves up the sound space differently.

buildup.text: Phonemes are the smallest units that change meaning. Swap one sound in 'bat' and you get 'pat'—a different word.

discovery.text: Babies can hear every phoneme in every language. By 12 months, they've pruned down to just their native set.

twist.text: Japanese speakers can't easily distinguish 'r' from 'l'—not because they can't hear, but because their brain merged them.

climax.text: Your native language literally reshapes your auditory cortex within the first year of life.

punchline.text: By age one, your ears have already chosen a language.

quiz.question: What happens to babies' phoneme perception by 12 months?
options: They narrow to their native language sounds

details.summary: Phonemes are the smallest units of sound that distinguish meaning in a language. Changing one phoneme changes the word: bat becomes pat. Languages differ in their phoneme inventories, from 11 to over 100.
details.whyItMatters: Phonemes are the building blocks of spoken language. Understanding them explains accents, reading difficulties, and why foreign sounds are hard to hear.
takeaways: Phonemes are sounds that change word meaning
Languages use different subsets of possible speech sounds
Perceptual narrowing tunes infant ears to native phonemes

faq.question: Why can't adults hear some foreign language sounds?
faq.answer: By age one, the brain has tuned to native phoneme categories, merging foreign distinctions that don't matter in the native language. Japanese speakers merge English R and L because Japanese has a single category for that sound space. The perceptual categories, once set, resist reorganization.

faq.question: How many phonemes does English have?
faq.answer: English has roughly 44 phonemes, 24 consonants and 20 vowels, though the exact count varies with dialect. This is moderate; Hawaiian has about 13 while some Khoisan languages have over 100 including clicks. The number of phonemes tends to be larger in languages with longer histories of contact.
